title: We Should All Be Najya Now
author: Chris Stewart
source: the revolution will be literate (citizen.substack.com), September 25, 2026
summary: Chris Stewart, a longtime sparring partner of Nikole Hannah-Jones on integration and school choice, calls her new essay the most honest thing he has read from the integration side of the debate. He argues that reforms for Black children should be judged by the standard Black educators set long before Brown v. Board: rigorous teaching, honest assessment, and adults who answer to families, not the racial makeup of the room. Stewart recovers that tradition, from post-emancipation literacy gains and Anna Julia Cooper's M Street High School to Vanessa Siddle Walker's account of Black educators' professional networks, and he recounts how desegregation cost tens of thousands of Black teachers their jobs. He finds that almost nothing that failed Najya concerned racial composition, and he criticizes both a left fixated on integration and a right for which choice without accountability is the whole of civil rights. The piece ends by linking Najya to Barbara Johns, two Black girls who asked adults for an education and were answered with a cause.
points: Stewart argues integration orthodoxy discounts Black agency by implying Black schools fail for lack of white students.
Literacy among Black Americans rose from about one in twenty to more than half within 35 years of emancipation, without white classmates.
After Brown, tens of thousands of Black teachers lost jobs and Black principals were demoted or dismissed.
He supports all school options, public and private, but only if each is held accountable for whether children learn.
Najya's own phone search exposed in an afternoon what adults had failed to tell her in nine years.
quotes: Any reform for Black children should be judged by the standard Black educators set long before Brown v. Board, which means rigorous teaching, honest assessment, and adults who answer to families, rather than by the racial makeup of the room.
The reason Nikole’s stubborn push for integration and her aversion to school choice grated on me is that they seem to discount Black agency.

Tens of thousands of Black teachers lost their jobs across the South and border states after Brown, Black principals were demoted or dismissed at staggering rates, and the profession Siddle Walker describes was dissolved into systems that had no use for it.
The most useful part of the essay is its catalog of what went wrong, and almost none of it concerns a classroom’s racial makeup.

Options without accountability gave us Unison’s A’s in algebra. Accountability without options gave us P.S. 307, where a family with a New York Times byline couldn’t get a graded worksheet out of the building.
Two Black girls, three generations apart, asked the adults for an education, and both times the adults answered with a cause.
I would add that there is no excuse either, when the most important fact about any school can be found by a seventh grader with a phone.
